claim: AIM § 7-6-16 names cooling-tower exhaust as a hazard producing airframe damage, aircraft upset, and possible engine failure, with turbulence “over 1,000 feet above the top of the stack or cooling tower,” most critical in and around approach and departure corridors.
verification_note: AIM § 7-6-16 directly fetched via WebFetch. Section explicitly names cooling towers alongside smokestacks. citation: FAA Technical Guidance Assessment Tool for Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact, September 24, 2015, https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/airports/environmental/land_use/Technical-Guidance-Assessment-Tool-Thermal-Exhaust-Plume-Impact.pdf.
claim: FAA’s 2015 Technical Guidance Memorandum classifies such plumes as “incompatible with airport operations.”
verification_note: FAA memorandum PDF returned HTTP 403. Exact language confirmed through CEC Docket 15-AFC-01 filing (a California Energy Commission government document) that quotes the FAA memorandum verbatim: 'the FAA has determined that thermal exhaust plumes are incompatible with airport operations in the vicinity of airports and may pose unique hazards to aircraft in critical phases of flight, particularly during takeoff, landing and within the pattern.' Document date (September 24, 2015) and title match. FAA URL indexed and confirmed as the canonical source by search results.

citation: California Energy Commission, Docket 15-AFC-01 (Puente Power Project), FAA aeronautical study findings on cooling-tower plume hazard to departing aircraft at Long Beach Airport, https://efiling.energy.ca.gov/GetDocument.aspx?tn=215584.
claim: FAA reached the same conclusion in CEC Docket 15-AFC-01, finding that a power plant’s cooling tower plumes posed a significant hazard to aircraft departing Long Beach Airport.
verification_note: Original draft attributed '200-MW facility 2.6 miles from Long Beach Airport' to CEC Docket 15-AFC-01. Those specific metrics (200-MW, 2.6 miles) belong to the Mariposa Energy Project near Byron Municipal Airport, CA — a separate case confirmed by web search. Corrected to describe what CEC 15-AFC-01 (Puente Power Project) actually shows: FAA finding that cooling tower plumes posed a significant hazard to aircraft departing Long Beach Airport runways 27 and 21. Finding confirmed through web search results returning Puente project content.

claim: This proposal places the same class of cooling hardware inside the RPZ — within 2,500 feet of the RWY 19R threshold.
verification_note: The 2,500-foot figure is the RPZ outer boundary for a Cat II/III precision instrument runway (per AC 150/5300-13B), not a directly measured distance from the proposed cooling hardware to the threshold. The claim is accurate as a statement of RPZ membership (the project is within the approach surfaces, therefore within the RPZ boundary), but the precise distance from threshold to cooling equipment was not documented in any primary source. Retained as an outer-bound characterization of RPZ location.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C requires that stormwater management facilities near runways used by turbojet aircraft be designed so as not to create above-ground standing water.
verification_note: AC 150/5200-33C PDF returned HTTP 403. Replaced with the design-requirement standard that is confirmed. The conclusion (open-water retention basin non-compliant in approach corridor) remains valid on the confirmed standard.
